opus-5.5.text:
What I find most striking is that the model gets better at reasoning simply by thinking longer internally, without producing any extra tokens. With our recurrent-depth architecture, we have a block of layers that we can iterate as many times as we want at test time. On tasks that really require reasoning, like math word problems such as GSM8K, or some of the ARC-style questions, performance keeps climbing as we add more recurrent iterations. It's a fairly small model, about three and a half billion parameters, trained on a modest amount of data by today's standards, but when you let it recur enough, it starts behaving on some benchmarks like a much larger model.

The other thing that surprised me is how differentiated the behavior is. On tasks that are more about recall or simple knowledge, like basic factual questions, it saturates very quickly. A few iterations are enough and extra compute doesn't help much. But on the reasoning-heavy tasks it keeps benefiting from more depth. So the model, in a sense, has learned to use compute where it actually matters, and that suggests you could build in adaptive compute pretty naturally, where it stops early on easy tokens and keeps thinking on hard ones.

And then there's the question of what's actually happening in that latent space. When we looked at the trajectories of the hidden states, we saw some really interesting structure, things like orbits or circular patterns when the model is working through arithmetic, and states that slide in particular directions. It's not verbalizing a chain of thought. It's doing something in continuous space that we never explicitly trained it to do, and that, to me, is maybe the most exciting part. It suggests there's a lot of reasoning that doesn't need to be put into words at all.

fable-5.1.text:
What I find most striking is that the model learned to use test-time compute in a way we never explicitly told it to. We trained this recurrent-depth model, Huginn, where the same block of layers is iterated many times, and the number of iterations is sampled randomly during training. So the model never sees a signal like "this is a hard problem, loop more." And yet when you look at it at inference, it does behave adaptively. On easy tokens, the latent state converges quickly and basically stops changing. On harder tokens, particularly in math or code, it keeps moving for many more iterations before it settles down.

The other thing that surprised me is how much performance you can pull out of a relatively small model just by scaling depth at test time. This is a 3.5 billion parameter model, and if you give it 32 or 64 recurrences, on reasoning benchmarks like GSM8K it ends up competitive with models that have far more parameters. The recurrence is doing work that would normally require either a bigger network or a long chain-of-thought in tokens. And it does this in latent space, without having to verbalize every intermediate step, which I think is interesting because a lot of reasoning isn't naturally expressible in language anyway.

And then there's the behavior of the latent state itself. When we visualize the trajectories, you see things we didn't design. Some tokens converge to a fixed point, as you'd expect. But others orbit, they oscillate in a periodic way, and some tokens, especially numerical ones, trace out structures that look almost like the model is sliding along a dimension while it's computing. That the model discovers these different computational regimes on its own, from a very generic training setup, is the part that I keep coming back to.

astra-6.text:
What I find striking is that you can give the model more computation by letting it run through the same recurrent block additional times, and that can improve its reasoning without adding parameters or generating a longer chain of thought. So there’s a distinction between how much the model says and how much computation it does before saying it.

That doesn’t necessarily mean we know what’s happening internally. I’d be careful about calling each recurrence a reasoning step. But it gives us an interesting way to study whether a model can use additional computation to refine a representation and arrive at a better answer.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find striking is that the model can spend more computation on a problem without having to express every intermediate step in words. It can revisit the same internal representation, refine it, and only then produce an answer. So the amount of computation isn’t tied directly to the number of tokens it generates.

That gives us an interesting way to think about reasoning: how much can happen in the model’s latent state, and how much needs to happen through an explicit chain of thought? I wouldn’t say recurrence alone answers that question, but it gives us a way to study it.
